This article covers the history of **women in the United States Senate** and various milestones achieved by female senators. It includes a list of all women who have served in the Senate, a list of current female senators, and a list of states represented by women in the Senate. The first female U.S. senator, [Rebecca Latimer Felton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rebecca_Latimer_Felton "Rebecca Latimer Felton"), represented [Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_(U.S._state) "Georgia (U.S. state)") for a single day in 1922, and the first woman elected to the Senate, [Hattie Caraway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hattie_Caraway "Hattie Caraway"), was elected from [Arkansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arkansas "Arkansas") in 1932. Sixty-five women have served in the Senate throughout American history.

Currently (since July 14, 2026), 27 women are serving in the Senate, which is the most women who have ever served in the Senate at the same time.

[Barbara Mikulski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbara_Mikulski "Barbara Mikulski") (born July 20, 1936) is the oldest living former female member of the Senate at the age of 90.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Women_in_the_United_States_Senate&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

See also: [List of the first women holders of political offices in the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_the_first_women_holders_of_political_offices_in_the_United_States "List of the first women holders of political offices in the United States")

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d3/Rebecca_Felton_-_desk.jpg/250px-Rebecca_Felton_-_desk.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Rebecca_Felton_-_desk.jpg)

[Rebecca Latimer Felton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rebecca_Latimer_Felton "Rebecca Latimer Felton"), the first woman in the United States Senate, who served representing Georgia for a single day in 1922.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_in_the_United_States_Senate#cite_note-auto3-1)

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5d/Yearofthewoman.jpg/250px-Yearofthewoman.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Yearofthewoman.jpg)

One woman ([Barbara Mikulski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbara_Mikulski "Barbara Mikulski")) was reelected and four women were [elected to the Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1992_United_States_Senate_elections "1992 United States Senate elections") in 1992, the "[Year of the Woman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Year_of_the_Woman "Year of the Woman")," Left to right: Senators [Patty Murray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patty_Murray "Patty Murray"), [Carol Moseley Braun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Moseley_Braun "Carol Moseley Braun"), Mikulski, [Dianne Feinstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dianne_Feinstein "Dianne Feinstein"), and [Barbara Boxer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbara_Boxer "Barbara Boxer").

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5b/Senate_women_March_2009.jpg/250px-Senate_women_March_2009.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Senate_women_March_2009.jpg)

By the [111th United States Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/111th_United_States_Congress "111th United States Congress") (2009–2011), the number of female senators had increased to 17, including 4 Republicans and 13 Democrats

The first time a woman was nominated for the Senate was in 1893 in Wyoming, where women have had the vote since 1869. The nomination happened through a [party caucus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Party_caucus "Party caucus"), since this was before 1913 when the [Seventeenth Amendment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seventeenth_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution "Seventeenth Amendment to the United States Constitution") established popular elections for senators. Mary Jane Bartlett was nominated by the Wyoming [Populists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Party_(United_States) "People's Party (United States)"), receiving their unanimous nomination. However, the Wyoming legislature was deadlocked for weeks of voting on their senators: Republicans, Democrats, and Populists mostly voted for their own candidates. Bartlett received all six populist votes on a number of ballots in the legislature, but time ran out to choose the senator, and Wyoming ended up serving with only one senator, rather than two, that term.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_in_the_United_States_Senate#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_in_the_United_States_Senate#cite_note-3)

The first woman to serve in the U.S. Senate was [Rebecca Latimer Felton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rebecca_Latimer_Felton "Rebecca Latimer Felton"); she represented [Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_senators_from_Georgia "List of United States senators from Georgia") for one day as a symbolic gesture in 1922.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_in_the_United_States_Senate#cite_note-auto3-1) Ten years later, [Hattie Caraway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hattie_Caraway "Hattie Caraway") became the first woman to win election to the Senate, representing [Arkansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_senators_from_Arkansas "List of United States senators from Arkansas"). She first filled the vacancy caused by her husband's death, and then was elected to two full terms.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_in_the_United_States_Senate#cite_note-4) In 1949, [Margaret Chase Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Chase_Smith "Margaret Chase Smith") began her service in the Senate; she was the first woman to serve in both the [House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_of_Representatives "United States House of Representatives") and Senate.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_in_the_United_States_Senate#cite_note-congress-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_in_the_United_States_Senate#cite_note-umaine-6) Her [1960](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1960_United_States_Senate_elections "1960 United States Senate elections") reelection bid resulted in Chase Smith winning the nation's first-ever Senate election with two female major party nominees; the other major party nominee was [Lucia Cormier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucia_Cormier "Lucia Cormier").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_in_the_United_States_Senate#cite_note-7) In 1978, [Muriel Humphrey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muriel_Humphrey "Muriel Humphrey") became the first former [Second Lady](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Lady_of_the_United_States "Second Lady of the United States") to serve in the United States Senate, after her husband [Hubert Humphrey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey "Hubert Humphrey")'s death in office. She was appointed to fill his Senate seat; she served for less than one year and declined to run for election to the seat.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_in_the_United_States_Senate#cite_note-8) Also in 1978, [Nancy Kassebaum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Kassebaum "Nancy Kassebaum") became the first woman ever elected to a full term in the Senate without succeeding her spouse.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_in_the_United_States_Senate#cite_note-auto4-9) Of the female senators who preceded Kassebaum: Appointed instead of elected applies to [Rebecca Latimer Felton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rebecca_Latimer_Felton "Rebecca Latimer Felton"),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_in_the_United_States_Senate#cite_note-auto3-1)[Rose McConnell Long](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rose_McConnell_Long "Rose McConnell Long"), [Dixie Bibb Graves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dixie_Bibb_Graves "Dixie Bibb Graves"), [Vera C. Bushfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vera_C._Bushfield "Vera C. Bushfield"), [Eva Bowring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eva_Bowring "Eva Bowring"), [Elaine S. Edwards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_S._Edwards "Elaine S. Edwards"), [Muriel Humphrey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muriel_Humphrey "Muriel Humphrey"), and [Maryon Pittman Allen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maryon_Pittman_Allen "Maryon Pittman Allen"); [Gladys Pyle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gladys_Pyle "Gladys Pyle") (R-SD) and [Hazel Abel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hazel_Abel "Hazel Abel") (R-NE), were elected, but not to full terms (i.e., to complete terms where the previous senator had died or resigned, not to new six-year terms); [Hattie Caraway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hattie_Caraway "Hattie Caraway") and [Maurine Brown Neuberger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurine_Brown_Neuberger "Maurine Brown Neuberger") were both elected to full six-year terms, but their husbands had held the seat previously. [Margaret Chase Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Chase_Smith "Margaret Chase Smith")'s (R-ME) husband never served in the Senate, but he did serve in the House. When he died, Margaret won the ensuing election. Of the appointed senators, Long, Bushfield, Humphrey, and Allen were all appointed to fill out part of the terms of their deceased husbands, while Graves and Edwards were appointed by their husbands, the governor of their states at the time. However, Kassebaum's [father](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alf_Landon "Alf Landon") was a former governor of Kansas, which means that the first woman to be elected to the Senate without any family connections was [Paula Hawkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Hawkins_(politician) "Paula Hawkins (politician)"), who was elected in 1980 to represent Florida. Since Kassebaum assumed office in December 1978, there has been at least one woman in the Senate. The first woman to be elected to the Senate without any family connections was Florida Republican [Paula Hawkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Hawkins_(politician) "Paula Hawkins (politician)"), elected in [1980](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980_United_States_Senate_election_in_Florida "1980 United States Senate election in Florida"). She was also the first female member of the [Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_Jesus_Christ_of_Latter-day_Saints "Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints") elected to the United States Senate.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_in_the_United_States_Senate#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_in_the_United_States_Senate#cite_note-11) In 1990, there were still few women in the Senate as compared to the number of women in the House. The trend of few women in the Senate began to change in the wake of the [Clarence Thomas Supreme Court nomination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clarence_Thomas_Supreme_Court_nomination "Clarence Thomas Supreme Court nomination") hearings and the subsequent election of the [103rd United States Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/103rd_United_States_Congress "103rd United States Congress") in [1992](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1992_United_States_Senate_election "1992 United States Senate election"), which was dubbed the "[Year of the Woman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Year_of_the_Woman "Year of the Woman")."[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_in_the_United_States_Senate#cite_note-12)[Barbara Mikulski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbara_Mikulski "Barbara Mikulski") was reelected and four new Democratic women were elected to the Senate. They were [Patty Murray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patty_Murray "Patty Murray") of [Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_senators_from_Washington "List of United States senators from Washington"), [Carol Moseley Braun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Moseley_Braun "Carol Moseley Braun") of [Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_senators_from_Illinois "List of United States senators from Illinois"), [Dianne Feinstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dianne_Feinstein "Dianne Feinstein") of [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_senators_from_California "List of United States senators from California"), and [Barbara Boxer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbara_Boxer "Barbara Boxer") of California. [Carol Moseley Braun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Moseley_Braun "Carol Moseley Braun") was the first Black woman and [woman of color](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Person_of_color "Person of color") to serve in the Senate and the first woman to defeat an incumbent senator after she won the 1992 Democratic primary election over [Alan J. Dixon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_J._Dixon "Alan J. Dixon"). Later in 1992, Feinstein was the first woman to defeat an incumbent senator from a different party when she defeated [John Seymour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_F._Seymour "John F. Seymour") in a special election. Feinstein entered the Senate the same year as the first female Jewish senator.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_in_the_United_States_Senate#cite_note-autogenerated1-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_in_the_United_States_Senate#cite_note-congress1-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_in_the_United_States_Senate#cite_note-congress2-15)

Bathroom facilities for women in the Senate on the [Senate chamber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Capitol "United States Capitol") level were first provided in 1992.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_in_the_United_States_Senate#cite_note-Plaskow-16) Women were not allowed to wear pants on the Senate floor until 1993.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_in_the_United_States_Senate#cite_note-chicagotribune2004-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_in_the_United_States_Senate#cite_note-rollcall1-18) In 1993, Senators [Barbara Mikulski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbara_Mikulski "Barbara Mikulski") and [Carol Moseley Braun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Moseley_Braun "Carol Moseley Braun") wore pants onto the floor in defiance of the rule, and female support staff followed soon after, with the rule being amended later that year by Senate Sergeant-at-Arms Martha Pope to allow women to wear pants on the floor so long as they also wore a jacket.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_in_the_United_States_Senate#cite_note-chicagotribune2004-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_in_the_United_States_Senate#cite_note-rollcall1-18)

The first time two female senators from the same state served concurrently was in 1993; [Dianne Feinstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dianne_Feinstein "Dianne Feinstein") and [Barbara Boxer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbara_Boxer "Barbara Boxer") of California were both elected in 1992, with Feinstein taking office that same year (as the result of a special election) and Boxer taking office in 1993. Boxer served until 2016, when she retired, and Feinstein was then joined by [Kamala Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamala_Harris "Kamala Harris"). In June 1993, [Kay Bailey Hutchison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kay_Bailey_Hutchison "Kay Bailey Hutchison") won a special election in Texas, and joined Kassebaum as a fellow female [Republican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)") senator. These additions significantly diminished the popular perception of the Senate as an exclusive "boys' club". Since 1992, there has been at least one new woman elected to the Senate every two years, with the exception of [2004](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_United_States_Senate_elections "2004 United States Senate elections") (Lisa Murkowski was elected for the first time in 2004, but had been appointed to the seat since 2002).

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ab/Female_senators_DNC_2008.jpg/330px-Female_senators_DNC_2008.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Female_senators_DNC_2008.jpg)

Eight Democratic women senators appear at the [2008 Democratic Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Democratic_National_Convention "2008 Democratic National Convention") in Denver. It has become a tradition at Democratic conventions for incumbent women senators to appear on opening night.

[Olympia Snowe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympia_Snowe "Olympia Snowe") of [Maine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_senators_from_Maine "List of United States senators from Maine") assumed office in the Senate in 1995, having previously served in the [US House of Representatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_of_Representatives "United States House of Representatives") and both houses of the [Maine state legislature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maine_state_legislature "Maine state legislature"). She was the first woman (later joined by [Debbie Stabenow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Stabenow "Debbie Stabenow") of [Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan "Michigan"), [Kyrsten Sinema](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kyrsten_Sinema "Kyrsten Sinema") of [Arizona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arizona "Arizona"), and [Cynthia Lummis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cynthia_Lummis "Cynthia Lummis") of [Wyoming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyoming "Wyoming")) to have served in both houses of a state legislature and both houses of the federal legislature. In 2000, Stabenow and [Maria Cantwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Cantwell "Maria Cantwell") became the first women to defeat incumbent elected senators in a general election, defeating Senators [Spencer Abraham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spencer_Abraham "Spencer Abraham") and [Slade Gorton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slade_Gorton "Slade Gorton") respectively.[[n 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_in_the_United_States_Senate#cite_note-19)[Hillary Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hillary_Clinton "Hillary Clinton") is the first [First Lady](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Lady_of_the_United_States "First Lady of the United States") to run for or win a Senate seat. Clinton took office in the Senate in 2001, becoming the first female senator from [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_senators_from_New_York "List of United States senators from New York"), and served until 2009, when she resigned to become the 67th [United States Secretary of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_State "United States Secretary of State"), under [President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States")[Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama"). She was replaced by [Kirsten Gillibrand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirsten_Gillibrand "Kirsten Gillibrand"), who has been elected three times and was herself a candidate for president in the [2020 Democratic Party presidential primaries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Democratic_Party_presidential_primaries "2020 Democratic Party presidential primaries").

In 2008, Democrat [Kay Hagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kay_Hagan "Kay Hagan") of [North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Carolina "North Carolina") became the first woman to defeat a female incumbent, [Elizabeth Dole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_Dole "Elizabeth Dole"). Upon the opening of the [112th United States Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/112th_United_States_Congress "112th United States Congress") in 2011, New Hampshire Democrat [Jeanne Shaheen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeanne_Shaheen "Jeanne Shaheen") was joined by newly elected Republican [Kelly Ayotte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelly_Ayotte "Kelly Ayotte"), making up the first Senate delegation of two women belonging to different parties.

Patty Murray holds the record as the longest serving woman senator. As a serving senator, her record is continuously extended.

In 2012, a record five new female senators were elected. This beat the record of four new female senators from 1992 and set the record of five new women and eleven female senators in one Senate class. The five new women were Democrats [Tammy Baldwin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tammy_Baldwin "Tammy Baldwin") of [Wisconsin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_senators_from_Wisconsin "List of United States senators from Wisconsin"), [Heidi Heitkamp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heidi_Heitkamp "Heidi Heitkamp") of [North Dakota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_senators_from_North_Dakota "List of United States senators from North Dakota"), [Mazie Hirono](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mazie_Hirono "Mazie Hirono") of [Hawaii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_senators_from_Hawaii "List of United States senators from Hawaii"), [Elizabeth Warren](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_Warren "Elizabeth Warren") of [Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_senators_from_Massachusetts "List of United States senators from Massachusetts"), and Republican [Deb Fischer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deb_Fischer "Deb Fischer") of [Nebraska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_senators_from_Nebraska "List of United States senators from Nebraska"). Hirono was the first Asian-American woman and first Buddhist elected to the Senate,[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_in_the_United_States_Senate#cite_note-20)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_in_the_United_States_Senate#cite_note-21) and Baldwin was the first openly gay person elected to the Senate.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_in_the_United_States_Senate#cite_note-22)

In 2014, [Joni Ernst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joni_Ernst "Joni Ernst") was elected as the first female combat veteran to serve in the Senate.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_in_the_United_States_Senate#cite_note-23) In 2016, [Catherine Cortez Masto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catherine_Cortez_Masto "Catherine Cortez Masto") was elected as the first Latina senator,[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_in_the_United_States_Senate#cite_note-24) while [Tammy Duckworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tammy_Duckworth "Tammy Duckworth") was elected as the first female double amputee in the Senate.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_in_the_United_States_Senate#cite_note-25) In a June 2016 primary election, as a result of California's recent establishment of the [top-two primary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Top-two_primary "Top-two primary"), [Attorney General of California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attorney_General_of_California "Attorney General of California")[Kamala Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamala_Harris "Kamala Harris") and U.S. Representative [Loretta Sanchez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loretta_Sanchez "Loretta Sanchez") became the first women of the same party to advance to a Senate general election. In November 2016, Harris became the first woman to defeat a woman of the same party in a Senate general election.

In [2016](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election "2016 United States presidential election"), Hillary Clinton became the first former female senator to win a major party's nomination for President of the United States. Despite winning a plurality of the popular vote, she ultimately lost to [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump").

Starting in 2017, United States Senators [Jeanne Shaheen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeanne_Shaheen "Jeanne Shaheen") and [Maggie Hassan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maggie_Hassan "Maggie Hassan") of [New Hampshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_senators_from_New_Hampshire "List of United States senators from New Hampshire"), have held the distinction of being the first and second women elected as both the governor of a state and a United States senator from a state; both served as [Governor of New Hampshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_New_Hampshire "Governor of New Hampshire") before their time in the Senate. Additionally, in 2024, former U.S. Senator [Kelly Ayotte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelly_Ayotte "Kelly Ayotte") was elected Governor of New Hampshire, becoming the third woman and first Republican woman to hold this distinction.

In 2018, [Kyrsten Sinema](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kyrsten_Sinema "Kyrsten Sinema") was elected as [Arizona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_senators_from_Arizona "List of United States senators from Arizona")'s first female senator and the first openly bisexual senator from any state, defeating [Martha McSally](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_McSally "Martha McSally").[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_in_the_United_States_Senate#cite_note-nbc_181113-26) Two weeks later, Arizona Governor [Doug Ducey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doug_Ducey "Doug Ducey") announced that he would appoint McSally to Arizona's other Senate seat, which was becoming vacant with the resignation of [Jon Kyl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jon_Kyl "Jon Kyl"), who was appointed earlier in the year following the death of [John McCain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McCain "John McCain"). Sinema and McSally have been the only concurrently serving female senators to have previously faced off against each other in a Senate election. McSally's appointment from the Senate ended in December 2020 after losing that year's special election to Democrat [Mark Kelly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Kelly "Mark Kelly").

Also in 2018, [Jacky Rosen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacky_Rosen "Jacky Rosen") made political history as the first female one-term outgoing U.S. representative ever elected to the Senate,[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_in_the_United_States_Senate#cite_note-27) and [Tammy Duckworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tammy_Duckworth "Tammy Duckworth") became the first sitting senator to give birth.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_in_the_United_States_Senate#cite_note-autogenerated2-28)

In 2023, Patty Murray became the first woman to serve as [president pro tempore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_pro_tempore_of_the_United_States_Senate "President pro tempore of the United States Senate"), a role traditionally given to the most senior member of the majority party in the United States Senate. Dianne Feinstein was the most senior Democratic senator but declined to serve. This made Murray the third person [in line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_presidential_line_of_succession "United States presidential line of succession") to become president, after the [vice president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_the_United_States "Vice President of the United States") and the [Speaker of the House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speaker_of_the_United_States_House_of_Representatives "Speaker of the United States House of Representatives").[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_in_the_United_States_Senate#cite_note-29) Later that year, Feinstein became the first female senator to die in office.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_in_the_United_States_Senate#cite_note-senatorsdiedinoffice-30)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_in_the_United_States_Senate#cite_note-31)

In 2025, [Angela Alsobrooks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angela_Alsobrooks "Angela Alsobrooks") was sworn in alongside [Lisa Blunt Rochester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisa_Blunt_Rochester "Lisa Blunt Rochester"), making the [119th United States Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/119th_United_States_Congress "119th United States Congress") the first in which two Black women served in the U.S. Senate simutaneously.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_in_the_United_States_Senate#cite_note-32)

Following the death of [Lindsey Graham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lindsey_Graham "Lindsey Graham") in 2026,[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_in_the_United_States_Senate#cite_note-auto-33)[Darline Graham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darline_Graham "Darline Graham"), sworn in on July 14 of that year, became the first woman to represent South Carolina in the Senate,[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_in_the_United_States_Senate#cite_note-34) the first sister to replace her brother in Congress,[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_in_the_United_States_Senate#cite_note-auto2-35) and also the first sibling to replace a deceased senator.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_in_the_United_States_Senate#cite_note-auto-33) Her appointment marks the first time 27 women have served concurrently in the Senate, the highest number in its history.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_in_the_United_States_Senate#cite_note-auto1-36)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_in_the_United_States_Senate#cite_note-37) This includes a record high number of eleven Republican women serving at once, of which Graham herself is one.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_in_the_United_States_Senate#cite_note-auto1-36)

As of 2025, 64 women have served in the United States Senate since its establishment in 1789.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_in_the_United_States_Senate#cite_note-38) Cumulatively, 39 female U.S. senators have been Democrats, while 26 have been Republicans and one is an independent. As of 2023, no female U.S. senator has ever won election to the House after her Senate term, resigned from a state governorship for the purpose of a Senate appointment by her successor, also won election as an independent or to represent more than one state in non-consecutive elections, served both seats of a state at different times, or represented a [third party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_party_(U.S._politics) "Third party (U.S. politics)") in her career. In December 2022, Senator Kyrsten Sinema became the first female senator to switch her party affiliation while in office.

Some female U.S. senators have later run for U.S. president or vice president (see [list of female United States presidential and vice presidential candidates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_female_United_States_presidential_and_vice_presidential_candidates "List of female United States presidential and vice presidential candidates")). In 2020, [Kamala Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamala_Harris "Kamala Harris") became the first female senator, current or former, to win her [vice presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election "2020 United States presidential election") bid and become the first female [President of the United States Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presiding_Officer_of_the_United_States_Senate "Presiding Officer of the United States Senate").

## Election, selection, and family

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Women_in_the_United_States_Senate&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Election, selection, and family")]

Women are much less likely than men to decide to run for election, despite generally having the same chances of winning elections as male counterparts. Research by [Jennifer Lawless](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jennifer_Lawless "Jennifer Lawless") and Richard Fox shines light on a few possible reasons. Women report much less enthusiasm for the motions of campaigning (such as fundraising or attending rallies) than men. They are more likely than men to decide not to campaign based on lack of resources. They are also much more likely than men to view themselves as lacking credentials, and time (even women with full-time jobs report spending more time on household chores than men). Finally, they are more likely than men to view races as competitive.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_in_the_United_States_Senate#cite_note-39)

Before 2001, a plurality of women joined the U.S. Senate through appointment following the death or resignation of a husband or father who previously held the seat. An example is [Muriel Humphrey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muriel_Humphrey "Muriel Humphrey") (D-MN), the widow of former senator and [Vice President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_the_United_States "Vice President of the United States")[Hubert Humphrey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Humphrey "Hubert Humphrey"); she was appointed to fill his seat until a special election was held (in which she did not run). However, with the election of three women in 2000, the balance shifted; more women have now entered service as a senator by winning elections than by being appointed.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Recent examples of selection include [Jean Carnahan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Carnahan "Jean Carnahan") and [Lisa Murkowski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisa_Murkowski "Lisa Murkowski"). In [2000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_United_States_Senate_elections "2000 United States Senate elections"), [Jean Carnahan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Carnahan "Jean Carnahan") (D-MO) was appointed to fill the Senate seat won by her recently deceased husband, [Mel Carnahan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel_Carnahan "Mel Carnahan"), who was killed in a plane crash a month before the election. Carnahan, even though dead, defeated the incumbent senator, [John Ashcroft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Ashcroft "John Ashcroft"). Carnahan's widow was named to fill his seat by [Governor of Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_governors_of_Missouri "List of governors of Missouri")[Roger Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_B._Wilson "Roger B. Wilson") until a special election was held. However, she lost the subsequent [2002 special election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_United_States_Senate_elections "2002 United States Senate elections") to fill out the rest of the six-year term. In 2002, Lisa Murkowski (R-AK) was appointed by her father [Governor of Alaska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_governors_of_Alaska "List of governors of Alaska")[Frank Murkowski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Murkowski "Frank Murkowski"), who had resigned from the Senate to become governor, to serve the remaining two years of his term. Lisa Murkowski defeated former governor Tony Knowles in her election bid in [2004](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_United_States_Senate_elections "2004 United States Senate elections").

Two recent members of the Senate brought with them a combination of name recognition resulting from the political careers of their famous husbands and their own substantial experience in public affairs. The first, former senator [Elizabeth Dole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_Dole "Elizabeth Dole") (R-NC), was married to former [Senate Majority Leader](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_Majority_Leader "Senate Majority Leader") and 1996 Republican presidential candidate [Bob Dole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Dole "Bob Dole") (R-KS) and served as [United States Secretary of Transportation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Transportation "United States Secretary of Transportation") under President [Ronald Reagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Reagan "Ronald Reagan") and [Secretary of Labor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_of_Labor "Secretary of Labor") under President [George H. W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_H._W._Bush "George H. W. Bush"); she later ran a losing bid for the Republican presidential nomination in 2000. The other, former senator [Hillary Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hillary_Clinton "Hillary Clinton") (D-NY), wife of former president [Bill Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Clinton "Bill Clinton"), was [First Lady of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Lady_of_the_United_States "First Lady of the United States") and First Lady of Arkansas before taking her seat in 2000. She too ran an [unsuccessful campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Democratic_Party_presidential_primaries "2008 Democratic Party presidential primaries") for her party's presidential nomination in 2008; she resigned in 2009 to become the [secretary of state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_State "United States Secretary of State") for the eventual victor of that election, [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama"). In 2016, she ran a [successful campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Democratic_Party_presidential_primaries "2016 Democratic Party presidential primaries") for her party's presidential nomination, eventually losing in the general election to Republican nominee [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump").

The first woman ever elected to a full term in the Senate without succeeding her spouse was [Nancy Kassebaum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Kassebaum "Nancy Kassebaum"),[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_in_the_United_States_Senate#cite_note-auto4-9) although she was the daughter of former Kansas governor and one-time presidential candidate [Alf Landon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alf_Landon "Alf Landon"). After retiring from the Senate, she married former senator [Howard Baker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howard_Baker "Howard Baker").

Among the women elected or appointed in Senate history, by stature, [Barbara Boxer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbara_Boxer "Barbara Boxer") (D-CA) and [Barbara Mikulski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbara_Mikulski "Barbara Mikulski") (D-MD) are the shortest, at 4 feet 11 inches (1.50 m), whereas [Kelly Loeffler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelly_Loeffler "Kelly Loeffler") (R-GA) is the tallest, at 5 feet 11 inches (1.80 m).[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_in_the_United_States_Senate#cite_note-40)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_in_the_United_States_Senate#cite_note-41)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_in_the_United_States_Senate#cite_note-42)

# 17 states haven’t had a female U.S. senator, and 18 haven’t had a woman governor

[](https://www.pewresearch.org/?p=191228)*   X

By[Katherine Schaeffer](https://www.pewresearch.org/staff/katherine-schaeffer/)

If Kamala Harris wins the presidency this November, she will be the first woman ever elected to the highest political office of the United States.

There could also be similar firsts in political contests around the country: Five races for U.S. Senate and two for governor feature a major-party nominee who, if elected, would be the first woman in their state to hold the office. And in Minnesota, a woman will ascend to the governorship for the first time if current Gov. Tim Walz is elected as Harris’ vice president.

How we did this

If elected, Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris would be the first woman in the top political office in the United States. We conducted this analysis to determine how many Senate and governor’s races could result in similar firsts.

For this analysis, we used data from[U.S. Senate historical records](https://www.senate.gov/senators/ListofWomenSenators.htm), the [Rutgers University Center for American Women and Politics](https://cawp.rutgers.edu/) and recent news reports.

[![Image 3: A map showing that 17 states have never been represented by a woman in the U.S. Senate.](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2024/10/SR_24.10.31_women-leaders_1.png?w=640)](https://www.pewresearch.org/?attachment_id=191234)
Overall, 17 states have never had a female senator, according to a Pew Research Center analysis of Senate historical records. This fall, Senate races in Delaware, Indiana, New Mexico, Rhode Island and Utah each feature a woman nominee who could become the state’s first.

Three of these candidates ([Lisa Blunt Rochester](https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2024/10/05/lisa-blunt-rochester-black-woman-senate/) of Delaware, [Valerie McCray](https://www.wbaa.org/local-news/2024-05-07/valerie-mccray-wins-democratic-u-s-senate-primary-making-indiana-history) of Indiana and [Caroline Gleich](https://www.deseret.com/utah/2024/08/27/caroline-gleich-running-to-replace-mitt-romney-utah-senate/) of Utah) are Democrats, and two ([Nella Domenici](https://www.aol.com/heinrich-battles-domenici-hold-onto-233400342.html) of New Mexico and [Patricia Morgan](https://rhodeislandcurrent.com/2024/09/24/name-recognition-remains-a-challenge-for-morgans-u-s-senate-bid/) of Rhode Island) are Republicans.

Blunt Rochester and McCray would also be the first Black senators to represent their respective states.

[![Image 4: A map showing that women have held governships in about two-thirds of states.](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2024/10/SR_24.10.31_women-leaders_2.png?w=640)](https://www.pewresearch.org/?attachment_id=191233)
Among the 18 states that have never had a woman governor, two – Indiana and Missouri – have a woman on the ballot in this year’s general election. [Jennifer McCormick](https://indianacapitalchronicle.com/2024/10/07/democrat-jennifer-mccormick-runs-on-optimism-embracing-republican-past/) of Indiana and [Crystal Quade](https://missouriindependent.com/2024/08/06/crystal-quade-captures-democratic-nomination-for-missouri-governor/) of Missouri are both Democratic nominees.

And in Minnesota, Lt. Gov. [Peggy Flanagan](https://www.npr.org/2024/08/23/nx-s1-5078569/peggy-flanagan-minnesota-indigenous-walz-harris-trump-election) will take over as governor if Walz is elected vice president. That would make her the first woman and the first Native American person to hold the office.

Five states have not had a woman senator _or_ a woman governor: Colorado, Idaho, Indiana, Pennsylvania and Virginia.

Women have served in numerous statewide [executive and legislative offices](https://cawpdata.rutgers.edu/women-elected-officials/position?current=2&yearend_filter=All&level%5B%5D=Statewide&items_per_page=50) over the decades, including in all the states where they have not yet held Senate seats or governorships. And every state has [sent at least one woman](https://www.npr.org/2022/11/08/1134352130/vermont-balint-election-day-results-2022) to either the U.S. House of Representatives or the Senate.

#### Women in the 118th Senate

In the current Congress, women hold 25 of 100 Senate seats – [a record high](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2023/01/03/118th-congress-has-a-record-number-of-women/). They represent a total of 21 states. In Minnesota, Nevada, New Hampshire and Washington, both senators are women.

Fourteen of the 25 current senators are the first women to represent their state in the Senate. Their tenures vary: Washington Democrat [Patty Murray](https://awpc.cattcenter.iastate.edu/directory/patty-murray/) has served in the Senate since 1993, whereas Wyoming Republican [Cynthia Lummis](https://www.wyomingpublicmedia.org/politics/2020-11-03/cynthia-lummis-becomes-first-woman-to-win-wyoming-senate-seat) took office in 2021.

Fifteen current women senators are Democrats, nine are Republicans and one (Kyrsten Sinema of Arizona) is an independent. Looking at the Senate as a whole, women make up a larger share of the Democratic caucus (31%) than the Republican caucus (18%).

#### A century in the Senate

Women have served in the Senate for over a century. In 1922, [Rebecca Latimer Felton](http://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/history-archaeology/rebecca-latimer-felton-1835-1930), a suffragist from Georgia, became the first woman senator. She was appointed to a vacant seat and served for just one day.

[![Image 5: An area chart showing that 60 women have been U.S. senators.](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2024/10/SR_24.10.31_women-leaders_4.png?w=640)](https://www.pewresearch.org/?attachment_id=191235)
Since then, a total of 60 women have represented 33 states in the Senate, and most of them have served in recent decades. About three-quarters (46) first took office after 1980.

A little over half (19) of the states that have ever been represented by a woman in the Senate have sent more than one.

Four women have represented California in the Senate, the most from any state. In addition to Harris, who [represented the state](https://www.nytimes.com/2024/08/22/us/politics/kamala-harris-senate.html) from 2017 to 2021, this group includes two long-serving senators. Democrat [Dianne Feinstein](https://apnews.com/article/dianne-feinstein-dead-c831f3228ac44faa9653234570bb8ce9) took office in 1992 and served until her death in 2023, and [Barbara Boxer](https://bioguide.congress.gov/search/bio/B000711), also a Democrat, was in office from 1993 to 2017.

Alabama, Louisiana, Maine, Minnesota, Nebraska and New Hampshire have each sent three women to the Senate.

**_Related:_**[_22 states have ever elected a Black woman to Congress_](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2023/02/16/22-states-have-ever-elected-a-black-woman-to-congress/)

#### Women in the governor’s mansion

[![Image 6: An area chart showing that 49 women have been U.S. governors.](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2024/10/SR_24.10.31_women-leaders_3.png?w=640)](https://www.pewresearch.org/?attachment_id=191229)
Overall, 49 women have held the governorship in 32 states since 1925, when two women took the oath of office for the first time.

That year, [Nellie Tayloe Ross](https://www.nga.org/governor/nellie-tayloe-ross/) of Wyoming was nominated in a special election and won the governorship following the death of her husband, Gov. William Ross. [Miriam “Ma” Ferguson](https://texaspolitics.utexas.edu/archive/html/exec/governors/15.html) of Texas, the first woman ever chosen for the office in a general election, was sworn in just 15 days later.

Women currently serve as governors in 12 states. Eight are Democrats and four are Republicans.

Five of the current governors are the first women elected in their state: Democrats Janet Mills of Maine and Kathy Hochul of New York; and Republicans Kim Reynolds of Iowa, Kristi Noem of South Dakota and Sarah Huckabee Sanders of Arkansas.

In Arizona, five women have held the governorship since 1988 – by far the most from any state. In fact, three women served consecutively over a 17-year stretch, from Republican [Jane Hull’s](https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/jane-hull-first-woman-elected-arizona-governor-dies-at-84) ascension in 1997 until Republican [Jan Brewer](https://www.nga.org/governor/jan-brewer/) left office in 2015.

_CORRECTION (Nov. 1, 2024): This analysis has been updated to indicate that every state has been represented by a woman in either the U.S. House of Representatives or the U.S. Senate._

# 17 states haven’t had a female U.S. senator, and 18 haven’t had a woman governor

By[Katherine Schaeffer](https://www.pewresearch.org/staff/katherine-schaeffer/)

If Kamala Harris wins the presidency this November, she will be the first woman ever elected to the highest political office of the United States.

There could also be similar firsts in political contests around the country: Five races for U.S. Senate and two for governor feature a major-party nominee who, if elected, would be the first woman in their state to hold the office. And in Minnesota, a woman will ascend to the governorship for the first time if current Gov. Tim Walz is elected as Harris’ vice president.

How we did this

If elected, Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris would be the first woman in the top political office in the United States. We conducted this analysis to determine how many Senate and governor’s races could result in similar firsts.

For this analysis, we used data from[U.S. Senate historical records](https://www.senate.gov/senators/ListofWomenSenators.htm), the [Rutgers University Center for American Women and Politics](https://cawp.rutgers.edu/) and recent news reports.

[![Image 3: A map showing that 17 states have never been represented by a woman in the U.S. Senate.](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2024/10/SR_24.10.31_women-leaders_1.png?w=640)](https://www.pewresearch.org/?attachment_id=191234)
Overall, 17 states have never had a female senator, according to a Pew Research Center analysis of Senate historical records. This fall, Senate races in Delaware, Indiana, New Mexico, Rhode Island and Utah each feature a woman nominee who could become the state’s first.

Three of these candidates ([Lisa Blunt Rochester](https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2024/10/05/lisa-blunt-rochester-black-woman-senate/) of Delaware, [Valerie McCray](https://www.wbaa.org/local-news/2024-05-07/valerie-mccray-wins-democratic-u-s-senate-primary-making-indiana-history) of Indiana and [Caroline Gleich](https://www.deseret.com/utah/2024/08/27/caroline-gleich-running-to-replace-mitt-romney-utah-senate/) of Utah) are Democrats, and two ([Nella Domenici](https://www.aol.com/heinrich-battles-domenici-hold-onto-233400342.html) of New Mexico and [Patricia Morgan](https://rhodeislandcurrent.com/2024/09/24/name-recognition-remains-a-challenge-for-morgans-u-s-senate-bid/) of Rhode Island) are Republicans.

Blunt Rochester and McCray would also be the first Black senators to represent their respective states.

[![Image 4: A map showing that women have held governships in about two-thirds of states.](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2024/10/SR_24.10.31_women-leaders_2.png?w=640)](https://www.pewresearch.org/?attachment_id=191233)
Among the 18 states that have never had a woman governor, two – Indiana and Missouri – have a woman on the ballot in this year’s general election. [Jennifer McCormick](https://indianacapitalchronicle.com/2024/10/07/democrat-jennifer-mccormick-runs-on-optimism-embracing-republican-past/) of Indiana and [Crystal Quade](https://missouriindependent.com/2024/08/06/crystal-quade-captures-democratic-nomination-for-missouri-governor/) of Missouri are both Democratic nominees.

And in Minnesota, Lt. Gov. [Peggy Flanagan](https://www.npr.org/2024/08/23/nx-s1-5078569/peggy-flanagan-minnesota-indigenous-walz-harris-trump-election) will take over as governor if Walz is elected vice president. That would make her the first woman and the first Native American person to hold the office.

Five states have not had a woman senator _or_ a woman governor: Colorado, Idaho, Indiana, Pennsylvania and Virginia.

Women have served in numerous statewide [executive and legislative offices](https://cawpdata.rutgers.edu/women-elected-officials/position?current=2&yearend_filter=All&level%5B%5D=Statewide&items_per_page=50) over the decades, including in all the states where they have not yet held Senate seats or governorships. And every state has [sent at least one woman](https://www.npr.org/2022/11/08/1134352130/vermont-balint-election-day-results-2022) to either the U.S. House of Representatives or the Senate.

#### Women in the 118th Senate

In the current Congress, women hold 25 of 100 Senate seats – [a record high](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2023/01/03/118th-congress-has-a-record-number-of-women/). They represent a total of 21 states. In Minnesota, Nevada, New Hampshire and Washington, both senators are women.

Fourteen of the 25 current senators are the first women to represent their state in the Senate. Their tenures vary: Washington Democrat [Patty Murray](https://awpc.cattcenter.iastate.edu/directory/patty-murray/) has served in the Senate since 1993, whereas Wyoming Republican [Cynthia Lummis](https://www.wyomingpublicmedia.org/politics/2020-11-03/cynthia-lummis-becomes-first-woman-to-win-wyoming-senate-seat) took office in 2021.

Fifteen current women senators are Democrats, nine are Republicans and one (Kyrsten Sinema of Arizona) is an independent. Looking at the Senate as a whole, women make up a larger share of the Democratic caucus (31%) than the Republican caucus (18%).

#### A century in the Senate

Women have served in the Senate for over a century. In 1922, [Rebecca Latimer Felton](http://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/history-archaeology/rebecca-latimer-felton-1835-1930), a suffragist from Georgia, became the first woman senator. She was appointed to a vacant seat and served for just one day.

[![Image 5: An area chart showing that 60 women have been U.S. senators.](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2024/10/SR_24.10.31_women-leaders_4.png?w=640)](https://www.pewresearch.org/?attachment_id=191235)
Since then, a total of 60 women have represented 33 states in the Senate, and most of them have served in recent decades. About three-quarters (46) first took office after 1980.

A little over half (19) of the states that have ever been represented by a woman in the Senate have sent more than one.

Four women have represented California in the Senate, the most from any state. In addition to Harris, who [represented the state](https://www.nytimes.com/2024/08/22/us/politics/kamala-harris-senate.html) from 2017 to 2021, this group includes two long-serving senators. Democrat [Dianne Feinstein](https://apnews.com/article/dianne-feinstein-dead-c831f3228ac44faa9653234570bb8ce9) took office in 1992 and served until her death in 2023, and [Barbara Boxer](https://bioguide.congress.gov/search/bio/B000711), also a Democrat, was in office from 1993 to 2017.

Alabama, Louisiana, Maine, Minnesota, Nebraska and New Hampshire have each sent three women to the Senate.

**_Related:_**[_22 states have ever elected a Black woman to Congress_](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2023/02/16/22-states-have-ever-elected-a-black-woman-to-congress/)

#### Women in the governor’s mansion

[![Image 6: An area chart showing that 49 women have been U.S. governors.](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2024/10/SR_24.10.31_women-leaders_3.png?w=640)](https://www.pewresearch.org/?attachment_id=191229)
Overall, 49 women have held the governorship in 32 states since 1925, when two women took the oath of office for the first time.

That year, [Nellie Tayloe Ross](https://www.nga.org/governor/nellie-tayloe-ross/) of Wyoming was nominated in a special election and won the governorship following the death of her husband, Gov. William Ross. [Miriam “Ma” Ferguson](https://texaspolitics.utexas.edu/archive/html/exec/governors/15.html) of Texas, the first woman ever chosen for the office in a general election, was sworn in just 15 days later.

Women currently serve as governors in 12 states. Eight are Democrats and four are Republicans.

Five of the current governors are the first women elected in their state: Democrats Janet Mills of Maine and Kathy Hochul of New York; and Republicans Kim Reynolds of Iowa, Kristi Noem of South Dakota and Sarah Huckabee Sanders of Arkansas.

In Arizona, five women have held the governorship since 1988 – by far the most from any state. In fact, three women served consecutively over a 17-year stretch, from Republican [Jane Hull’s](https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/jane-hull-first-woman-elected-arizona-governor-dies-at-84) ascension in 1997 until Republican [Jan Brewer](https://www.nga.org/governor/jan-brewer/) left office in 2015.

[Presidential elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_presidential_election "United States presidential election") were held in the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") on November 8, 2016. The [Republican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)") ticket of businessman [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") and [Indiana governor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_Indiana "Governor of Indiana")[Mike Pence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Pence "Mike Pence") defeated the [Democratic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)") ticket of former [secretary of state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_State "United States Secretary of State")[Hillary Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hillary_Clinton "Hillary Clinton") and [Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia "Virginia") junior [senator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate")[Tim Kaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tim_Kaine "Tim Kaine"), in what was considered one of the biggest political [upsets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upset_(competition) "Upset (competition)") in American history.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-PoliticoUpset-4) It was the fifth and most recent presidential election in which the [winning candidate lost the popular vote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_presidential_elections_in_which_the_winner_lost_the_popular_vote "List of United States presidential elections in which the winner lost the popular vote").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-e2016-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-trumped-5)

Incumbent Democratic president [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama") was ineligible to run for a third term due to the term limits established by the [Twenty-second Amendment to the U.S. Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twenty-second_Amendment_to_the_U.S._Constitution "Twenty-second Amendment to the U.S. Constitution"). Clinton—wife of former president [Bill Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Clinton "Bill Clinton") and as such a former [first lady](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Lady_of_the_United_States "First Lady of the United States")—secured the nomination over U.S. senator [Bernie Sanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernie_Sanders "Bernie Sanders") in [the Democratic primary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Democratic_Party_presidential_primaries "2016 Democratic Party presidential primaries") and became the first female presidential nominee of a major American political party. Initially considered a [novelty candidate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Novelty_candidate "Novelty candidate"), Trump presented himself as a blunt-spoken political outsider and emerged as the [Republican front-runner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Republican_Party_presidential_primaries "2016 Republican Party presidential primaries"), defeating several notable opponents, including U.S. senators [Ted Cruz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ted_Cruz_2016_presidential_campaign "Ted Cruz 2016 presidential campaign") and [Marco Rubio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Rubio_2016_presidential_campaign "Marco Rubio 2016 presidential campaign"), as well as governors [John Kasich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Kasich_2016_presidential_campaign "John Kasich 2016 presidential campaign") and [Jeb Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeb_Bush_2016_presidential_campaign "Jeb Bush 2016 presidential campaign").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-6) Trump's [right-wing populist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Right-wing_populist "Right-wing populist") and [nationalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_nationalism_and_Trumpism "American nationalism and Trumpism") campaign promised to "[Make America Great Again](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Make_America_Great_Again "Make America Great Again")" and opposed [political correctness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_correctness "Political correctness") and many [US free trade agreements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_free_trade_agreements "US free trade agreements"),[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-7) while supporting a more hard-line approach on [illegal immigration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illegal_immigration_to_the_United_States "Illegal immigration to the United States"). Trump garnered extensive [free media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earned_media "Earned media") coverage due to his inflammatory comments.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-FreeMediaAdvantage-8)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-USNewsMedia-9) Clinton emphasized her extensive political experience; denounced Trump and half of his supporters as "[deplorable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basket_of_deplorables "Basket of deplorables")" bigots and extremists; and advocated the expansion of [Obama's policies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Barack_Obama "Presidency of Barack Obama"), stressing [racial equality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racial_equality "Racial equality"), [LGBT rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LGBT_rights_in_the_United_States "LGBT rights in the United States"), [women's rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feminism_in_the_United_States "Feminism in the United States"), and [inclusive capitalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inclusive_capitalism "Inclusive capitalism").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-offersecplan-10)

The tone of the election campaign was widely characterized as divisive, negative, and troubling.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-11)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-12)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-13) Trump faced controversy over [his views on race and immigration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racial_views_of_Donald_Trump "Racial views of Donald Trump"), incidents of [violence against protesters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protests_against_Donald_Trump#Trump's_reactions "Protests against Donald Trump") at his rallies,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-14)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-15)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-16) and numerous [sexual misconduct allegations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump_sexual_misconduct_allegations "Donald Trump sexual misconduct allegations") including the [_Access Hollywood_ tape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump_Access_Hollywood_tape "Donald Trump Access Hollywood tape"). Clinton's popularity and public image were tarnished by concerns about her ethics, trustworthiness,[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-17) and a controversy and subsequent [FBI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FBI "FBI") investigation regarding [her improper use of a private email server](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hillary_Clinton_email_controversy "Hillary Clinton email controversy") while serving as secretary of state, the latter of which received more media coverage than any other topic during the campaign.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-18)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-19) Clinton led in almost every nationwide and swing-state poll, with some predictive models giving her over a 90 percent chance of victory.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-20)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-21)

On election day, Trump over-performed his polls, winning several key [swing states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swing_state "Swing state") to achieve a majority in the [Electoral College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Electoral_College "United States Electoral College") while losing the nationwide popular vote by 2.87 million votes.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-22) Key to Trump's pivotal upset victory were his wins in the Democratic-leaning [Rust Belt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rust_Belt "Rust Belt") states of [Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election_in_Michigan "2016 United States presidential election in Michigan"), [Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election_in_Pennsylvania "2016 United States presidential election in Pennsylvania"), and [Wisconsin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election_in_Wisconsin "2016 United States presidential election in Wisconsin"), which he carried by fewer than 80,000 votes in the three "[blue wall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_wall_(United_States) "Blue wall (United States)")" states combined and gained a combined 46 electoral votes. Trump's surprise victories were perceived to have been assisted by Clinton's lack of campaigning in some swing states (especially Wisconsin),[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-23) the rightward shift of the white [working class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Working_class_in_the_United_States "Working class in the United States"),[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-Nate_Silver-24)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-25) as well as the influence of [Obama–Trump voters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obama%E2%80%93Trump_voters "Obama–Trump voters") and [Sanders–Trump voters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanders%E2%80%93Trump_voters "Sanders–Trump voters").[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-26)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-27)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-28) Ultimately, Trump received 304 electoral votes to Clinton's 227, as two [faithless electors defected](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faithless_electors_in_the_2016_United_States_presidential_election "Faithless electors in the 2016 United States presidential election") from Trump and five from Clinton. Trump was the first president with neither [prior public service nor military experience](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_presidents_of_the_United_States_by_previous_experience "List of presidents of the United States by previous experience").

With ballot access to the entire national electorate, [Libertarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libertarian_Party_(United_States) "Libertarian Party (United States)") nominee [Gary Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Johnson "Gary Johnson") received nearly 4.5 million votes (3.27%), the highest nationwide vote share for a third-party candidate since [Ross Perot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ross_Perot "Ross Perot") in [1996](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_United_States_presidential_election "1996 United States presidential election"),[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-29) while [Green Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Party_(United_States) "Green Party (United States)") nominee [Jill Stein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jill_Stein "Jill Stein") received almost 1.45 million votes (1.06%). Independent candidate [Evan McMullin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evan_McMullin "Evan McMullin") received [21.4%](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election_in_Utah "2016 United States presidential election in Utah") of the vote in his home state of Utah, the highest share of the vote for a non-major party candidate in any state since 1992.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-30)

On January 6, 2017, the [U.S. Intelligence Community](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Intelligence_Community "U.S. Intelligence Community") concluded that the [Russian government had interfered in the election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_interference_in_the_2016_United_States_elections "Russian interference in the 2016 United States elections")[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-31)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-32) in order to "undermine public faith in the U.S. democratic process, denigrate Secretary Clinton, and harm her electability and potential presidency".[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-33) A [Special Counsel investigation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mueller_special_counsel_investigation "Mueller special counsel investigation")[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-34)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-35) concluded in March 2019 that Russia had interfered "in sweeping and systematic fashion" in favor of Trump's candidacy but did not establish that members of the Trump campaign colluded with the Russian government.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-36)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-37)

## Background

Further information: [United States presidential election §Procedure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_presidential_election#Procedure "United States presidential election")

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8d/President_Barack_Obama.jpg/250px-President_Barack_Obama.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:President_Barack_Obama.jpg)

[Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama"), the incumbent president in 2016, whose second term expired at noon on January 20, 2017

President [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama"), a [Democrat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)") and former [U.S. senator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate") from [Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illinois "Illinois"), was ineligible to seek reelection to a third term due to the restrictions of the American presidential term limits established by the [Twenty-second Amendment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twenty-second_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution "Twenty-second Amendment to the United States Constitution").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-38)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-39)

Both the Democratic and Republican parties, as well as third parties such as the Green and Libertarian parties, held a series of [presidential primary elections and caucuses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_presidential_primary "United States presidential primary") that took place between February and June 2016, staggered among the 50 states, the [District of Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/District_of_Columbia "District of Columbia"), and [U.S. territories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Territories_of_the_United_States "Territories of the United States"). This nominating process was also an indirect election, where voters cast ballots for a slate of delegates to a political party's [nominating convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_presidential_nominating_convention "United States presidential nominating convention"), who in turn elected their party's presidential nominee. Speculation about the 2016 campaign began almost immediately following the 2012 campaign, with _[New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New\_York\_(magazine) "New York (magazine)")_ magazine declaring that the race had begun in an article published on November 8, two days after the 2012 election.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-40) On the same day, _[Politico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politico "Politico")_ released an article predicting that the 2016 general election would be between Clinton and former [Florida Governor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_Florida "Governor of Florida")[Jeb Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeb_Bush "Jeb Bush"), while an article in _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times "The New York Times")_ named [New Jersey Governor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_governors_of_New_Jersey "List of governors of New Jersey")[Chris Christie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Christie "Chris Christie") and Senator [Cory Booker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cory_Booker "Cory Booker") from [New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Jersey "New Jersey") as potential candidates.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-41)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-42)

## Nominations

### Republican Party

#### Primaries

Main article: [2016 Republican Party presidential primaries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Republican_Party_presidential_primaries "2016 Republican Party presidential primaries")

With seventeen major candidates entering the race, starting with [Ted Cruz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ted_Cruz "Ted Cruz") on March 23, 2015, this was the largest presidential primary field for any political party in American history,[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-43) before being overtaken by the 2020 Democratic presidential primaries.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-44)

Prior to the [Iowa caucuses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Iowa_Republican_presidential_caucuses "2016 Iowa Republican presidential caucuses") on February 1, 2016, Perry, Walker, Jindal, Graham, and Pataki withdrew due to low polling numbers. Despite leading many polls in Iowa, Trump came in second to Cruz, after which Huckabee, Paul, and Santorum withdrew due to poor performances at the ballot box. Following a sizable victory for Trump in the [New Hampshire primary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_New_Hampshire_Republican_presidential_primary "2016 New Hampshire Republican presidential primary"), Christie, Fiorina, and Gilmore abandoned the race. Bush followed suit after scoring fourth place to Trump, Rubio, and Cruz in [South Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_South_Carolina_Republican_presidential_primary "2016 South Carolina Republican presidential primary"). On March 1, the first of four "[Super Tuesday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Tuesday "Super Tuesday")" primaries, Rubio won his first contest in [Minnesota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Minnesota_Republican_presidential_caucuses "2016 Minnesota Republican presidential caucuses"), Cruz won [Alaska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Alaska_Republican_presidential_caucuses "2016 Alaska Republican presidential caucuses"), [Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Oklahoma_Republican_presidential_primary "2016 Oklahoma Republican presidential primary"), and his home state of [Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Texas_Republican_presidential_primary "2016 Texas Republican presidential primary"), and Trump won the other seven states that voted. Failing to gain traction, Carson suspended his campaign a few days later.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-45) On March 15, the second "Super Tuesday", Kasich won his only contest in his home state of [Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Ohio_Republican_presidential_primary "2016 Ohio Republican presidential primary"), and Trump won five primaries including [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Florida_Republican_presidential_primary "2016 Florida Republican presidential primary"). Rubio suspended his campaign after losing his home state.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-Rubio-46)

Between March 16 and May 3, only three candidates remained in the race: Trump, Cruz, and Kasich. Cruz won the most delegates in four Western contests and in [Wisconsin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Wisconsin_Republican_presidential_primary "2016 Wisconsin Republican presidential primary"), keeping a credible path to denying Trump the nomination on the first ballot with 1,237 delegates. Trump then augmented his lead by scoring landslide victories in his home state of [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_New_York_Republican_presidential_primary "2016 New York Republican presidential primary") and five Northeastern states in April, followed by a decisive victory in [Indiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Indiana_Republican_presidential_primary "2016 Indiana Republican presidential primary") on May 3, securing all 57 of the state's delegates. Without any further chances of forcing a [contested convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brokered_convention "Brokered convention"), both Cruz[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-47) and Kasich[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-48) suspended their campaigns. Trump remained the only active candidate and was declared the presumptive Republican nominee by [Republican National Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_National_Committee "Republican National Committee") chairman [Reince Priebus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reince_Priebus "Reince Priebus") on the evening of May 3.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-49)

A 2018 study found that media coverage of Trump led to increased public support for him during the primaries. The study showed that Trump received nearly $2 billion in free media, more than double any other candidate. Political scientist [John M. Sides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_M._Sides "John M. Sides") argued that Trump's polling surge was "almost certainly" due to frequent media coverage of his campaign. Sides concluded "Trump is surging in the polls because the news media has consistently focused on him since he announced his candidacy on June 16".[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-50) Prior to clinching the Republican nomination, Trump received little support from establishment Republicans.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-51)

#### Candidates

Main article: [2016 Republican Party presidential candidates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Republican_Party_presidential_candidates "2016 Republican Party presidential candidates")

Major candidates were determined by the various media based on common consensus. The following were invited to sanctioned televised debates based on their poll ratings.
