[Presidential elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_presidential_election "United States presidential election") were held in the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") on November 8, 2016. The [Republican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)") ticket of businessman [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") and [Indiana governor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_Indiana "Governor of Indiana")[Mike Pence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Pence "Mike Pence") defeated the [Democratic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)") ticket of former [secretary of state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_State "United States Secretary of State")[Hillary Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hillary_Clinton "Hillary Clinton") and [Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia "Virginia") junior [senator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate")[Tim Kaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tim_Kaine "Tim Kaine"), in what was considered one of the biggest political [upsets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upset_(competition) "Upset (competition)") in American history.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-PoliticoUpset-4) It was the fifth and most recent presidential election in which the [winning candidate lost the popular vote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_presidential_elections_in_which_the_winner_lost_the_popular_vote "List of United States presidential elections in which the winner lost the popular vote").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-e2016-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-trumped-5)

Incumbent Democratic president [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama") was ineligible to run for a third term due to the term limits established by the [Twenty-second Amendment to the U.S. Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twenty-second_Amendment_to_the_U.S._Constitution "Twenty-second Amendment to the U.S. Constitution"). Clinton—wife of former president [Bill Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Clinton "Bill Clinton") and as such a former [first lady](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Lady_of_the_United_States "First Lady of the United States")—secured the nomination over U.S. senator [Bernie Sanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernie_Sanders "Bernie Sanders") in [the Democratic primary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Democratic_Party_presidential_primaries "2016 Democratic Party presidential primaries") and became the first female presidential nominee of a major American political party. Initially considered a [novelty candidate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Novelty_candidate "Novelty candidate"), Trump presented himself as a blunt-spoken political outsider and emerged as the [Republican front-runner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Republican_Party_presidential_primaries "2016 Republican Party presidential primaries"), defeating several notable opponents, including U.S. senators [Ted Cruz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ted_Cruz_2016_presidential_campaign "Ted Cruz 2016 presidential campaign") and [Marco Rubio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Rubio_2016_presidential_campaign "Marco Rubio 2016 presidential campaign"), as well as governors [John Kasich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Kasich_2016_presidential_campaign "John Kasich 2016 presidential campaign") and [Jeb Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeb_Bush_2016_presidential_campaign "Jeb Bush 2016 presidential campaign").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-6) Trump's [right-wing populist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Right-wing_populist "Right-wing populist") and [nationalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_nationalism_and_Trumpism "American nationalism and Trumpism") campaign promised to "[Make America Great Again](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Make_America_Great_Again "Make America Great Again")" and opposed [political correctness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_correctness "Political correctness") and many [US free trade agreements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_free_trade_agreements "US free trade agreements"),[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-7) while supporting a more hard-line approach on [illegal immigration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illegal_immigration_to_the_United_States "Illegal immigration to the United States"). Trump garnered extensive [free media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earned_media "Earned media") coverage due to his inflammatory comments.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-FreeMediaAdvantage-8)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-USNewsMedia-9) Clinton emphasized her extensive political experience; denounced Trump and half of his supporters as "[deplorable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basket_of_deplorables "Basket of deplorables")" bigots and extremists; and advocated the expansion of [Obama's policies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Barack_Obama "Presidency of Barack Obama"), stressing [racial equality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racial_equality "Racial equality"), [LGBT rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LGBT_rights_in_the_United_States "LGBT rights in the United States"), [women's rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feminism_in_the_United_States "Feminism in the United States"), and [inclusive capitalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inclusive_capitalism "Inclusive capitalism").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-offersecplan-10)

The tone of the election campaign was widely characterized as divisive, negative, and troubling.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-11)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-12)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-13) Trump faced controversy over [his views on race and immigration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racial_views_of_Donald_Trump "Racial views of Donald Trump"), incidents of [violence against protesters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protests_against_Donald_Trump#Trump's_reactions "Protests against Donald Trump") at his rallies,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-14)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-15)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-16) and numerous [sexual misconduct allegations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump_sexual_misconduct_allegations "Donald Trump sexual misconduct allegations") including the [_Access Hollywood_ tape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump_Access_Hollywood_tape "Donald Trump Access Hollywood tape"). Clinton's popularity and public image were tarnished by concerns about her ethics, trustworthiness,[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-17) and a controversy and subsequent [FBI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FBI "FBI") investigation regarding [her improper use of a private email server](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hillary_Clinton_email_controversy "Hillary Clinton email controversy") while serving as secretary of state, the latter of which received more media coverage than any other topic during the campaign.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-18)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-19) Clinton led in almost every nationwide and swing-state poll, with some predictive models giving her over a 90 percent chance of victory.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-20)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-21)

On election day, Trump over-performed his polls, winning several key [swing states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swing_state "Swing state") to achieve a majority in the [Electoral College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Electoral_College "United States Electoral College") while losing the nationwide popular vote by 2.87 million votes.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-22) Key to Trump's pivotal upset victory were his wins in the Democratic-leaning [Rust Belt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rust_Belt "Rust Belt") states of [Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election_in_Michigan "2016 United States presidential election in Michigan"), [Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election_in_Pennsylvania "2016 United States presidential election in Pennsylvania"), and [Wisconsin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election_in_Wisconsin "2016 United States presidential election in Wisconsin"), which he carried by fewer than 80,000 votes in the three "[blue wall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_wall_(United_States) "Blue wall (United States)")" states combined and gained a combined 46 electoral votes. Trump's surprise victories were perceived to have been assisted by Clinton's lack of campaigning in some swing states (especially Wisconsin),[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-23) the rightward shift of the white [working class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Working_class_in_the_United_States "Working class in the United States"),[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-Nate_Silver-24)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-25) as well as the influence of [Obama–Trump voters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obama%E2%80%93Trump_voters "Obama–Trump voters") and [Sanders–Trump voters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanders%E2%80%93Trump_voters "Sanders–Trump voters").[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-26)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-27)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-28) Ultimately, Trump received 304 electoral votes to Clinton's 227, as two [faithless electors defected](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faithless_electors_in_the_2016_United_States_presidential_election "Faithless electors in the 2016 United States presidential election") from Trump and five from Clinton. Trump was the first president with neither [prior public service nor military experience](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_presidents_of_the_United_States_by_previous_experience "List of presidents of the United States by previous experience").

With ballot access to the entire national electorate, [Libertarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libertarian_Party_(United_States) "Libertarian Party (United States)") nominee [Gary Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Johnson "Gary Johnson") received nearly 4.5 million votes (3.27%), the highest nationwide vote share for a third-party candidate since [Ross Perot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ross_Perot "Ross Perot") in [1996](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_United_States_presidential_election "1996 United States presidential election"),[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-29) while [Green Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Party_(United_States) "Green Party (United States)") nominee [Jill Stein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jill_Stein "Jill Stein") received almost 1.45 million votes (1.06%). Independent candidate [Evan McMullin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evan_McMullin "Evan McMullin") received [21.4%](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election_in_Utah "2016 United States presidential election in Utah") of the vote in his home state of Utah, the highest share of the vote for a non-major party candidate in any state since 1992.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-30)

On January 6, 2017, the [U.S. Intelligence Community](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Intelligence_Community "U.S. Intelligence Community") concluded that the [Russian government had interfered in the election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_interference_in_the_2016_United_States_elections "Russian interference in the 2016 United States elections")[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-31)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-32) in order to "undermine public faith in the U.S. democratic process, denigrate Secretary Clinton, and harm her electability and potential presidency".[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-33) A [Special Counsel investigation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mueller_special_counsel_investigation "Mueller special counsel investigation")[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-34)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-35) concluded in March 2019 that Russia had interfered "in sweeping and systematic fashion" in favor of Trump's candidacy but did not establish that members of the Trump campaign colluded with the Russian government.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-36)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-37)

## Background

Further information: [United States presidential election §Procedure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_presidential_election#Procedure "United States presidential election")

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8d/President_Barack_Obama.jpg/250px-President_Barack_Obama.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:President_Barack_Obama.jpg)

[Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama"), the incumbent president in 2016, whose second term expired at noon on January 20, 2017

President [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama"), a [Democrat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)") and former [U.S. senator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate") from [Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illinois "Illinois"), was ineligible to seek reelection to a third term due to the restrictions of the American presidential term limits established by the [Twenty-second Amendment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twenty-second_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution "Twenty-second Amendment to the United States Constitution").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-38)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-39)

Both the Democratic and Republican parties, as well as third parties such as the Green and Libertarian parties, held a series of [presidential primary elections and caucuses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_presidential_primary "United States presidential primary") that took place between February and June 2016, staggered among the 50 states, the [District of Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/District_of_Columbia "District of Columbia"), and [U.S. territories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Territories_of_the_United_States "Territories of the United States"). This nominating process was also an indirect election, where voters cast ballots for a slate of delegates to a political party's [nominating convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_presidential_nominating_convention "United States presidential nominating convention"), who in turn elected their party's presidential nominee. Speculation about the 2016 campaign began almost immediately following the 2012 campaign, with _[New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New\_York\_(magazine) "New York (magazine)")_ magazine declaring that the race had begun in an article published on November 8, two days after the 2012 election.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-40) On the same day, _[Politico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politico "Politico")_ released an article predicting that the 2016 general election would be between Clinton and former [Florida Governor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_Florida "Governor of Florida")[Jeb Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeb_Bush "Jeb Bush"), while an article in _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times "The New York Times")_ named [New Jersey Governor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_governors_of_New_Jersey "List of governors of New Jersey")[Chris Christie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Christie "Chris Christie") and Senator [Cory Booker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cory_Booker "Cory Booker") from [New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Jersey "New Jersey") as potential candidates.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-41)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-42)

## Nominations

### Republican Party

#### Primaries

Main article: [2016 Republican Party presidential primaries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Republican_Party_presidential_primaries "2016 Republican Party presidential primaries")

With seventeen major candidates entering the race, starting with [Ted Cruz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ted_Cruz "Ted Cruz") on March 23, 2015, this was the largest presidential primary field for any political party in American history,[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-43) before being overtaken by the 2020 Democratic presidential primaries.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-44)

Prior to the [Iowa caucuses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Iowa_Republican_presidential_caucuses "2016 Iowa Republican presidential caucuses") on February 1, 2016, Perry, Walker, Jindal, Graham, and Pataki withdrew due to low polling numbers. Despite leading many polls in Iowa, Trump came in second to Cruz, after which Huckabee, Paul, and Santorum withdrew due to poor performances at the ballot box. Following a sizable victory for Trump in the [New Hampshire primary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_New_Hampshire_Republican_presidential_primary "2016 New Hampshire Republican presidential primary"), Christie, Fiorina, and Gilmore abandoned the race. Bush followed suit after scoring fourth place to Trump, Rubio, and Cruz in [South Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_South_Carolina_Republican_presidential_primary "2016 South Carolina Republican presidential primary"). On March 1, the first of four "[Super Tuesday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Tuesday "Super Tuesday")" primaries, Rubio won his first contest in [Minnesota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Minnesota_Republican_presidential_caucuses "2016 Minnesota Republican presidential caucuses"), Cruz won [Alaska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Alaska_Republican_presidential_caucuses "2016 Alaska Republican presidential caucuses"), [Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Oklahoma_Republican_presidential_primary "2016 Oklahoma Republican presidential primary"), and his home state of [Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Texas_Republican_presidential_primary "2016 Texas Republican presidential primary"), and Trump won the other seven states that voted. Failing to gain traction, Carson suspended his campaign a few days later.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-45) On March 15, the second "Super Tuesday", Kasich won his only contest in his home state of [Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Ohio_Republican_presidential_primary "2016 Ohio Republican presidential primary"), and Trump won five primaries including [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Florida_Republican_presidential_primary "2016 Florida Republican presidential primary"). Rubio suspended his campaign after losing his home state.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-Rubio-46)

Between March 16 and May 3, only three candidates remained in the race: Trump, Cruz, and Kasich. Cruz won the most delegates in four Western contests and in [Wisconsin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Wisconsin_Republican_presidential_primary "2016 Wisconsin Republican presidential primary"), keeping a credible path to denying Trump the nomination on the first ballot with 1,237 delegates. Trump then augmented his lead by scoring landslide victories in his home state of [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_New_York_Republican_presidential_primary "2016 New York Republican presidential primary") and five Northeastern states in April, followed by a decisive victory in [Indiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Indiana_Republican_presidential_primary "2016 Indiana Republican presidential primary") on May 3, securing all 57 of the state's delegates. Without any further chances of forcing a [contested convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brokered_convention "Brokered convention"), both Cruz[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-47) and Kasich[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-48) suspended their campaigns. Trump remained the only active candidate and was declared the presumptive Republican nominee by [Republican National Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_National_Committee "Republican National Committee") chairman [Reince Priebus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reince_Priebus "Reince Priebus") on the evening of May 3.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-49)

A 2018 study found that media coverage of Trump led to increased public support for him during the primaries. The study showed that Trump received nearly $2 billion in free media, more than double any other candidate. Political scientist [John M. Sides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_M._Sides "John M. Sides") argued that Trump's polling surge was "almost certainly" due to frequent media coverage of his campaign. Sides concluded "Trump is surging in the polls because the news media has consistently focused on him since he announced his candidacy on June 16".[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-50) Prior to clinching the Republican nomination, Trump received little support from establishment Republicans.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election#cite_note-51)
